sections.h2: How is property tax set in Washington?
sections.html:
Each county assessor values every parcel once a year, and each county treasurer collects the bill. Under RCW 84.40.020, real property is listed and assessed every year with reference to its value on January 1 of that year.

The standard of value is set by RCW 84.40.030: property is valued at 100 percent of its true and fair value in money. For a house, the assessor looks first at sales of the property or similar properties made within the past five years. The assessor must also respect existing zoning, so a value cannot be built on a use the land is not allowed to have. Land and structures are valued separately, and the two cannot add up to more than the property is worth as it stands.

When the assessor changes your value, a notice must go out no later than thirty days after the appraisal (RCW 84.40.045). It shows the old and new value, land and improvements listed separately, plus a short description of how to appeal. No such notice may be mailed between January 15 and February 15.

sections.h2: When are Washington property taxes due?
sections.html:
Washington taxes are due in two halves: the first on or before April 30 and the second on or before October 31. RCW 84.56.020 sets the calendar, and the half-and-half option applies when the tax on a parcel is $50 or more.

ItemWhat the statute says
First halfDue on or before April 30
Second halfDue on or before October 31
Tax statementsDistributed by March 15 when budgets, levies and the tax roll are delivered on schedule
Interest, residential parcel with four or fewer units9 percent per year, computed monthly from delinquency, with no penalty
Interest, other property12 percent per year
Penalties on nonresidential, larger multifamily and personal property3 percent on tax delinquent June 1, plus 8 percent more on December 1

Source: RCW 84.56.020 (app.leg.wa.gov).

Payments sent by mail without a readable postmark, and payments from an automated check service, count as on time if they arrive within three business days of the due date. Treasurers may also offer payment agreements and accept partial payments, applied to the oldest delinquent year first unless you ask otherwise. Ask your county treasurer which options it runs.

sections.h2: How do I appeal a Washington property assessment?
sections.html:
File a petition with your county board of equalization on the state form. RCW 84.40.038 gives you whichever is latest of these deadlines:

  • July 1 of the year of the assessment.
  • Thirty days after the assessment or value change notice was mailed.
  • Thirty days after the assessor sent it electronically or told you it was available online.
  • A county-adopted window of up to sixty days.

A petition that is not on the prescribed form or not fully completed may be refused, so read the form before you send it. If you miss the date, the board may waive it when you file within a reasonable time and show good cause. The statute lists examples: a death or serious illness in the family, being away from your mailing address for more than fifteen of the allowed days when the deadline falls after July 1, wrong written advice from county staff, a flood or earthquake, or a postal delay the post office has documented. The board must waive the deadline if you were never sent a revaluation notice even though your area was revalued and your value did not change.

You and the assessor can also ask for a direct appeal to the state Board of Tax Appeals if the assessor, you, and a majority of the county board all agree. The state board may decline, and the county board then hears the case. The Board of Tax Appeals publishes appeal forms and a checklist for residential owners who want to go further than the county board.

If a bill comes due while your appeal is still open, ask the county treasurer how to handle the payment.

sections.h2: What tax relief can Washington homeowners get?
sections.html:
The main programs are an exemption, a deferral, and a grant for certain widows and widowers of veterans. The Department of Revenue describes each on its exemptions and deferrals page, and your county assessor takes the applications.

  • Senior, disability and veteran exemption. You must own and occupy your primary residence in Washington and have income at or below your county's threshold. You must also be at least 61 by December 31 of the assessment year, unable to work because of a disability, or a veteran with a qualifying VA rating. The reduction depends on income, home value and local levy rates, and renewal is required at least once every six years as the assessor decides.
  • Senior and disability deferral. Available to owner-occupants who are 60 or older, or retired because of disability, with enough equity to secure the state's interest. Deferred tax accrues 5 percent simple interest and must be repaid when the home is sold, the owner dies, or the home stops being the primary residence.
  • Widow or widower of a veteran. A grant that does not have to be repaid if the recipient lives in the home until at least December 15 of the year it is received.

Two related protections sit in the collection statutes. A treasurer may not sell a property that is eligible for deferral and instead must require the owner to file a declaration to defer (RCW 84.64.050(6)). And under RCW 84.56.020(19), an income-qualified owner who lives in a home already facing tax foreclosure can have outstanding interest and penalties waived once, starting about 60 days before the three-year mark.

Income limits differ by county. Ask your county assessor for the current threshold for your county before you decide whether to apply.

sections.h2: What happens when property taxes go unpaid in Washington?
sections.html:
Interest runs from the date of delinquency, and after three years the county moves toward foreclosure. RCW 84.64.050 directs the treasurer to issue certificates of delinquency once three years have passed from the date of delinquency, then foreclose the tax liens in the county's name. The treasurer must give notice to the owner and anyone with a recorded interest, who then has thirty days after service to appear and defend or pay what is due.

Before any sale, the treasurer must run a title search to confirm the legal description and the record titleholder, and that person is treated as the owner for notice purposes. The statute also bars a certificate of delinquency when the total delinquency is $100 or less, not counting interest and penalties, except on parcels a local government has declared a nuisance.

Treasurers must also tell delinquent owners where to get help, including the statewide foreclosure hotline recommended by the Washington State Housing Finance Commission. Roughly two years into a delinquency, the treasurer passes the owner's name and address to a homeownership resource center or other designated entity.

sections.h2: How are taxes and excise tax handled when I sell a Washington house?
sections.html:
The tax lien runs from January 1, so the year's bill follows the property until it is paid. RCW 84.60.020 says that when the sale agreement is silent, the seller is liable for the share of that year's tax that matches the part of the calendar year before the day of sale, and the buyer takes the rest. Most contracts state their own split, and escrow normally settles it at closing. If you owe back taxes, ask the county treasurer for a payoff figure that includes interest through the closing date.

Selling also triggers the real estate excise tax. The Department of Revenue's REET page says the seller usually pays it, it is due to the county treasurer on the date of sale, and an unpaid balance can become a lien on the property. For sales beginning January 1, 2027, the state portion is 1.1 percent of the price up to $551,000, 1.28 percent from there to $1,551,000, 2.75 percent to $3,051,000, and 3 percent above that. Local excise tax is added on top, and interest runs on unpaid tax after one month. Your closing agent will put the exact figure on the settlement statement.

Sellers who need to move quickly with taxes owed, repairs pending or a tenant in place can ask a cash buyer to price those items into an as-is offer. The settlement statement shows the tax payoff as a line item, so you see exactly what is taken from proceeds.

faqs.q: What is the deadline to appeal my Washington property value?
faqs.a: It is the latest of July 1, thirty days after the notice was mailed or sent electronically, or a county-adopted window of up to sixty days. The county board of equalization can waive a missed deadline for good cause, such as serious illness, a flood or a documented postal delay (RCW 84.40.038).

faqs.q: Can I pay Washington property tax in two payments?
faqs.a: Yes, when the tax on a parcel is $50 or more. Half is due by April 30 and the rest by October 31. Treasurers may also offer payment agreements or partial payments, so ask your county treasurer what is available.

faqs.q: How much interest do late Washington property taxes carry?
faqs.a: Residential parcels with four or fewer units pay 9 percent a year, computed monthly, with no penalty. Nonresidential property, larger multifamily buildings and personal property pay 12 percent, and the last two groups also face a 3 percent penalty on June 1 and 8 percent more on December 1.

faqs.q: Do I have to pay property tax if I qualify for a senior exemption or deferral?
faqs.a: An exemption reduces what you owe, based on income, home value and levy rates. A deferral postpones payment and adds 5 percent simple interest, which comes due when the home is sold, the owner dies, or the home stops being the primary residence. Your county assessor handles both applications.

faqs.q: Who pays property tax at closing when I sell my house in Washington?
faqs.a: The sale agreement decides. If it says nothing, the seller owes the share of the year's tax matching the days before the sale and the buyer owes the rest (RCW 84.60.020). Escrow usually calculates this on the settlement statement, along with the seller's real estate excise tax.
